disease_name_ja: 鎌状赤血球症急性胸部症候群

distillation_scope.manifold_definition: Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease, defined clinically by acute respiratory symptoms or chest pain with a new pulmonary infiltrate, without splitting first-layer manifolds by infectious, fat embolic, atelectatic, or vaso-occlusive trigger subtypes.
distillation_scope.subtype_policy: Trigger mechanisms are represented as latent mechanisms and risk/context modifiers, not as separate first-layer disease leaves.

latent_mechanisms.label: deoxygenation-driven HbS polymerization and erythrocyte sickling
latent_mechanisms.rationale: HbS polymerization and sickling are the required substrate that turns hypoxemia, inflammation, infection, and fat embolism into pulmonary vaso-occlusion.

latent_mechanisms.label: pulmonary microvascular vaso-occlusion and infarctive injury
latent_mechanisms.rationale: Pulmonary vaso-occlusion links chest pain, hypoxemia, new infiltrates, pleural reaction, pulmonary hypertension, and rapid respiratory decompensation.

latent_mechanisms.label: alveolar inflammation, atelectasis, and consolidation
latent_mechanisms.rationale: ACS is recognized at the bedside by new airspace infiltrates with fever, cough, dyspnea, tachypnea, or hypoxemia.

latent_mechanisms.label: hypoxemia-sickling positive feedback
latent_mechanisms.rationale: Hypoxemia increases erythrocyte sickling, which worsens pulmonary perfusion and gas exchange.

latent_mechanisms.label: systemic vaso-occlusive pain activity
latent_mechanisms.rationale: ACS often emerges during a vaso-occlusive pain episode with chest, rib, back, abdominal, or limb pain.

latent_mechanisms.label: hemolysis, anemia, and reduced oxygen delivery
latent_mechanisms.rationale: Sickle cell disease creates chronic hemolysis and anemia; acute ACS episodes may worsen anemia and oxygen delivery.

latent_mechanisms.label: infectious or sterile inflammatory trigger activity
latent_mechanisms.rationale: Bacterial, viral, and sterile inflammatory triggers can precipitate the same ACS manifold, but do not define separate first-layer leaves here.

latent_mechanisms.label: fat embolic and endothelial lung injury activity
latent_mechanisms.rationale: Bone marrow infarction and fat embolism are recognized ACS triggers, represented as mechanism activity rather than a split subtype.

latent_mechanisms.label: pulmonary vascular resistance and right-heart stress
latent_mechanisms.rationale: Severe ACS can acutely raise pulmonary vascular resistance, especially in patients with pre-existing pulmonary hypertension.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Sickled erythrocytes obstruct pulmonary microcirculation.
Lower oxygen tension increases HbS polymerization and sickling.
Respiratory infection or systemic inflammation can cause fever, airway inflammation, and airspace consolidation.
Fat embolic lung injury can produce diffuse inflammatory infiltrates and hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Pulmonary infarctive and pleural irritation commonly cause chest or rib pain.
Pleuritic pain supports pulmonary infarctive or pleural surface involvement.
ACS may arise during a vaso-occlusive pain crisis with abdominal pain.
Back or flank pain can be part of the concurrent vaso-occlusive crisis.
Extremity or bone pain reflects systemic vaso-occlusive activity.
New pulmonary infiltrate is central to ACS recognition, even when the trigger is not bacterial pneumonia.
Diffuse inflammatory or fat embolic ACS may appear as ground-glass opacity.
Pleural effusions often accompany lower-lobe ACS and severe pulmonary inflammation.
Fever is common in ACS, especially with infectious or inflammatory triggers.
Tactile or measured fever may be reported before or during ACS evolution.
Cough can accompany airway or parenchymal inflammation.
Leukocytosis is common in SCD inflammation and infection-triggered ACS.
Neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis may accompany ACS.
Inflammatory activity may raise CRP during ACS.
Procalcitonin may rise when bacterial infection is the trigger, but it is not required for the ACS leaf.
Pulmonary vaso-occlusion and impaired gas exchange produce dyspnea.
Airspace disease reduces ventilation and increases work of breathing.
ACS severity is often expressed by low oxygen saturation or new oxygen requirement.
Severe ACS can meet ARDS-level gas exchange impairment.
Increasing respiratory support tracks hypoxemic ACS severity.
Tachypnea is a physiologic response to hypoxemia and lung injury.
Severe ACS can rapidly become acute respiratory failure.
Worsening gas exchange increases near-term respiratory failure risk.
Severe ACS can evolve into ARDS.
Escalating oxygen failure increases risk of invasive ventilation.
Acute illness may worsen anemia on top of chronic SCD hemolysis.
Hematocrit generally follows hemoglobin in ACS with anemia.
Reticulocytosis reflects marrow response to hemolytic anemia.
Absolute reticulocyte count may rise with hemolysis if marrow response is intact.
LDH can rise with hemolysis and tissue injury.
Haptoglobin is often low in hemolysis.
Bilirubin can rise from hemolysis and hepatic stress.
Indirect hyperbilirubinemia supports hemolytic contribution.
Clinical jaundice can accompany hemolysis.
Pulmonary vascular obstruction and hypoxic vasoconstriction can worsen pulmonary hypertension.
Severe respiratory failure can become hypercapnic, especially with fatigue or ventilatory failure.
Hypercapnic or mixed respiratory/metabolic failure may lower arterial pH.
Right-heart strain and severe hypoxemia can lead to hemodynamic collapse.
Severe hypoxemia is a major proximate driver of ACS mortality.
Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, and shock raise fatality risk in severe ACS.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Fever is common but not required; absence of fever does not exclude ACS.
Captures tactile fever or febrile history when exact temperature is absent.
Tachycardia tracks fever, pain, hypoxemia, anemia, and stress.
Tachypnea is a common respiratory severity marker in ACS.
Hypotension is not typical for uncomplicated ACS, but may occur in shock, severe hypoxemia, sepsis overlap, or right-heart failure.
New desaturation is a high-value ACS severity signal.
0 none, 1 low-flow oxygen, 2 high-flow oxygen, 3 noninvasive ventilation, 4 invasive ventilation, 5 ECMO-level support.
Low PaO2/FiO2 captures severe gas exchange failure and ARDS-level ACS.
Arterial oxygen tension may be low despite supplemental oxygen.
PaCO2 may be low with tachypnea or high in ventilatory failure.
Severe ACS may cause respiratory or mixed acidosis; compensated patients may retain near-normal pH.
Captures bedside respiratory failure severity when blood gas detail is incomplete.
Dyspnea is common once lung involvement becomes clinically apparent.
Cough may be present, especially with infectious or inflammatory triggers, but is not required.
Chest, rib, or thoracic pain is a common ACS presentation and may precede radiographic change.
Pleuritic quality increases support for pulmonary/pleural involvement, but parent chest pain should carry the main finding.
Abdominal pain can accompany the vaso-occlusive crisis during which ACS appears.
Back or flank pain may reflect concurrent vaso-occlusion.
Pain crisis symptoms can precede or coexist with ACS.

axes.axis_name: New pulmonary infiltrate or consolidation extent
axes.clinical_interpretation: New infiltrate is central to ACS, but the axis is reused from pneumonia ontology because the measured radiographic concept is the same.
Ground-glass change can appear in diffuse inflammatory or fat embolic ACS, but many ACS cases show consolidation instead.
Pleural effusion supports severity or pleural reaction but is not required.

axes.axis_name: Pulmonary hypertension or acute right-heart strain activity
axes.clinical_interpretation: Pre-existing or acute pulmonary hypertension magnifies severe ACS risk.
Leukocytosis may reflect inflammation, infection, stress, or SCD baseline.
Neutrophilia can occur with inflammatory or infectious ACS triggers.
CRP can rise in ACS but is trigger-sensitive and not specific.
Higher procalcitonin supports bacterial trigger or sepsis overlap, not the ACS leaf itself.
Baseline SCD anemia is common; acute decline or severe anemia worsens oxygen delivery.
Hematocrit parallels hemoglobin in SCD anemia.
Reticulocytosis supports hemolytic anemia or marrow response in SCD.
Absolute reticulocyte count is separate from reticulocyte percentage and should not be conflated.
LDH may rise with hemolysis and tissue injury.
Low haptoglobin supports hemolysis but may already be low in chronic SCD.
Hyperbilirubinemia can reflect hemolysis or hepatobiliary overlap.
Indirect bilirubin helps separate hemolytic contribution from hepatic overlap when measured.
Jaundice may accompany hemolysis but is not required for ACS.
Renal injury is not defining for ACS but can accompany severe hypoxemia, shock, dehydration, or multiorgan sickle crisis.
BUN can rise in severe ACS with renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury.
Lactate may rise with hypoxemia, shock, or sepsis overlap; it is not specific to ACS.
Bicarbonate may fall in metabolic acidosis or remain near normal in isolated hypoxemia.
Event risk for clinically important acute respiratory failure.
ACS can evolve to ARDS, especially with diffuse bilateral infiltrates and very low PaO2/FiO2.

axes.axis_name: Need for invasive mechanical ventilation hazard
axes.clinical_interpretation: Ventilation risk rises with refractory hypoxemia, hypercapnia, severe work of breathing, or altered mental status.
AKI is a severity or overlap event, not a defining ACS feature.
Shock hazard increases in severe ACS with sepsis overlap, right-heart failure, or profound hypoxemia.

axes.axis_name: Mortality hazard in sickle cell acute chest syndrome
axes.clinical_interpretation: Lifespan outcome hazard driven by hypoxemia, ARDS, mechanical ventilation risk, pulmonary vascular stress, shock, and multiorgan overlap.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Stronger when infiltrates are bilateral, lower-lobe extensive, or accompanied by pulmonary vaso-occlusion.
axis_couplings.rationale: More airspace disease reduces gas exchange.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Best when oxygen delivery device and FiO2 are documented.
Most relevant when bilateral infiltrates and noncardiogenic respiratory failure are present.
axis_couplings.rationale: Very low PaO2/FiO2 signals ARDS-level severity.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Escalating oxygen support despite transfusion and respiratory care.
axis_couplings.rationale: Rising support requirement predicts invasive ventilation risk.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Hypercapnia due to ventilatory failure rather than permissive ventilator strategy.
axis_couplings.rationale: Hypercapnia and acidosis mark respiratory pump failure.
Acidemia raises urgency of ventilatory support.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Anemia primarily reduces oxygen content; saturation may remain relatively preserved unless lung disease coexists.
axis_couplings.rationale: Low hemoglobin worsens oxygen delivery and physiologic reserve in ACS.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Most important in known pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular dysfunction, or acute cor pulmonale.
axis_couplings.rationale: Right-heart stress can destabilize severe ACS.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Relevant when respiratory failure is not rapidly reversed.
axis_couplings.rationale: Respiratory failure is a proximate pathway to mortality.

axis_couplings.conditionality: ARDS-level gas exchange failure and diffuse bilateral infiltrates.
axis_couplings.rationale: ARDS is a major severe ACS complication.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Shock from sepsis overlap, right-heart failure, or profound hypoxemia.
axis_couplings.rationale: Hemodynamic collapse increases near-term death risk.

axis_couplings.conditionality: When creatinine rise is acute relative to SCD baseline or accompanied by oliguria.
axis_couplings.rationale: Creatinine rise is the measurable AKI expression.

effect_modifiers.rationale: Extensive shunt physiology may blunt oxygen response.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporary oxygenation support while definitive ACS drivers are treated.

treatments.drug: opioid analgesia with careful respiratory monitoring

effect_modifiers.rationale: Hypercapnia or somnolence increases risk from respiratory depressant dosing.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces pain and splinting while requiring monitoring for hypoventilation.
Addresses atelectasis and splinting components of ACS.

effect_modifiers.rationale: Higher bacterial probability increases expected antimicrobial effect.

treatments.context_specific_role: Treats plausible bacterial trigger while ACS trigger subtype remains uncertain.

effect_modifiers.rationale: Higher hemoglobin limits simple transfusion because hyperviscosity risk rises.
Cardiopulmonary disease increases risk from volume load.

treatments.context_specific_role: Improves oxygen-carrying capacity and dilutes HbS burden when anemia or moderate hypoxemia is present.

effect_modifiers.rationale: Severe oxygen requirement increases expected value of rapid HbS reduction.
Very low PaO2/FiO2 identifies severe gas exchange failure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapidly reduces HbS fraction and improves oxygen delivery in severe or progressive ACS.

treatments.drug: high-flow nasal oxygen or noninvasive ventilation

effect_modifiers.rationale: Severe acidemia may require invasive ventilation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bridges moderate to severe respiratory failure while transfusion and trigger therapy act.
Supports life-threatening respiratory failure while maintaining lung-protective strategy.

effect_modifiers.rationale: Right-heart physiology affects ECMO candidacy and management.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue gas-exchange support for refractory severe ACS or ACS-associated ARDS.

prior_effect.rationale: ACS is a complication of sickle cell disease or sickling hemoglobinopathy.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: SCD baseline hemoglobin is often below general-population background.
Chronic hemolysis can raise bilirubin outside acute ACS.

prior_effect.rationale: HbSS generally carries higher ACS risk than many milder sickling genotypes.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: HbSS commonly has lower baseline hemoglobin.
Higher sickling burden can worsen ACS severity.

prior_effect.rationale: HbSC can cause ACS even when previously undocumented.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: HbSC may have higher baseline hemoglobin than HbSS, so hyperviscosity risk matters.

prior_effect.rationale: ACS often develops during or shortly after vaso-occlusive pain crisis.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: VOC may present with abdominal pain.

prior_effect.rationale: Chronic airway disease increases ACS susceptibility and respiratory severity.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Pre-existing lung disease lowers oxygenation reserve.

prior_effect.rationale: Pulmonary hypertension does not define ACS but increases severity once ACS occurs.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Known pulmonary hypertension raises the baseline of this axis.
Right-heart vulnerability increases shock hazard in severe ACS.
Pulmonary vascular disease worsens severe ACS prognosis.

prior_effect.rationale: Respiratory viral infection can precipitate ACS but is not specific.

axis_response_modulation.rationale: Viral trigger may increase fever expression.
Viral lung inflammation may add to ACS infiltrates.

supportive_care.description: Serial pulse oximetry, respiratory effort assessment, and escalation planning.
supportive_care.rationale: ACS can deteriorate rapidly even after initially mild presentation.

supportive_care.description: Avoid dehydration while monitoring for pulmonary edema or right-heart strain.
supportive_care.rationale: Hydration may support VOC physiology, but overload can worsen lung disease.

supportive_care.description: Monitor for transfusion reactions, alloimmunization history, iron overload, and vascular access risks.
supportive_care.rationale: Transfusion and exchange transfusion are central ACS interventions but context-sensitive.

supportive_care.description: Evaluate bacterial, viral, fat embolic, pulmonary embolic, atelectatic, and cardiogenic mimics or triggers as external context or future co-manifolds.
supportive_care.rationale: Trigger workup can guide treatment while the first-layer ACS manifold remains trigger-agnostic.

quality_notes: No treatment ordering labels are used; treatment ranking is left to forward simulation and outcome scoring.
Confirmatory hemoglobin electrophoresis, culture, treatment response, and follow-up outcomes should live in case confirmatory or outcome sections, not in rankable observations.
Pneumonia, hypoxemia, respiratory failure, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusive pain axes are reused where the measured clinical concept is shared.
